title: Teaching It Back
keyIdea: After you learn something, teach it back in your own words, to a person or even a toy. Say the idea, give an example you made up, and say why. Where you get stuck is a gap: now you know what to find out next.

kid: You just learned something new. Now teach it to someone else. A grown-up, a friend or a teddy will do.
Use your own words. Do not just copy what the teacher said. Copying can sound right, even when you do not get it.
A good way to teach has three parts. Say the idea. Give an example you thought of. Then say why it happens.
Did you get stuck when Teddy asked why? Good! That is a gap. Now you know what to find out. Teach it again once you know.
adult: Teaching it back means explaining something new in your own words to someone else, or to a toy. Some call it learning by teaching. Studies of self-explanation and of learning by teaching show that putting ideas into words, and then answering questions, builds memory and understanding more than reading it again does.

The lab practises each part. Children choose the explanation that teaches Teddy rather than a word-for-word copy or a wrong idea, build an explanation from an idea, their own example and a reason, find where Pip gets stuck when Teddy asks why, test their own examples on a magnet, and choose the three key ideas from a lesson on bees.

Common mistakes come up often. Children repeat the teacher's exact words, which can sound right with no understanding behind it. They reuse the teacher's example instead of making one up. They give an example that does not fit, such as thinking a magnet pulls all metals. They see getting stuck as failure, when it shows what to learn next. And they fill a summary with small details instead of key ideas.

After school, ask your child to teach you one thing they learned, as if you knew nothing. Ask why, and then ask for an example of their own. If they get stuck, say, great, that is what we can find out, and look it up together.

familyTip: Once a week, let your child be the teacher. They teach you, or a toy, one thing from school for two minutes. Ask one why question and one for an example of their own, and praise them when they spot something they do not know yet.

practice.prompt: The teacher said, "Sound travels as vibrations." Which shows Ana really understands?
choices: When I hit a drum it shakes, and the shaking moves through the air to my ears
Sound travels as vibrations
Sound is loud
practice.hint: Which one uses her own words and her own example?
practice.explain: Ana explains it her own way, with a drum example. Repeating the exact words could just be copying.

practice.prompt: Leo teaches Teddy about the {n} times table. Teddy asks why, and Leo is stuck. What should Leo do?
choices: Find out, then teach it again
Make something up
Stop teaching
practice.hint: Getting stuck shows a gap. What fills a gap?
practice.explain: Being stuck on the {n} times table shows Leo what to learn next. He finds out, then teaches it again.

practice.prompt: Idea: some things dissolve in water. Which is an example you made up yourself?
choices: Sugar in my tea disappears when I stir it
The salt the teacher showed us
Sand in a bucket of water
practice.hint: It should be your own, and it must fit the idea.
practice.explain: Sugar in tea is your own example and it dissolves. Salt was the teacher's, and sand does not dissolve.

practice.prompt: You learned {n} facts about frogs. You can teach Teddy three. Which is a key idea?
choices: Frogs start life as tadpoles in water
The book had a green cover
My friend likes frogs
practice.hint: Which one helps Teddy understand frogs?
practice.explain: Out of {n} facts, frogs starting as tadpoles is a key idea. The book cover and your friend are small details.

pool.prompt: What does teaching it back mean?
choices: Explaining what you learned in your own words
Reading the page again
Copying the teacher's words
pool.hint: Think of Teddy. What did you do for him?
pool.explain: Teaching it back means explaining it yourself, to a person or a toy, in your own words.

pool.prompt: Who can you teach it back to?
choices: A grown-up, a friend or even a toy
Only a teacher
Only someone older than you
pool.hint: Pip taught Teddy. Does the listener have to be a person?
pool.explain: Anyone works, even a toy. Saying it out loud is what helps you learn.

pool.prompt: Mia gets stuck when her brother asks why. What does that show?
choices: A gap she can learn next
That she is bad at learning
That the question was silly
pool.hint: What did Pip do after getting stuck?
pool.explain: Getting stuck shows a gap. Now Mia knows exactly what to find out.

pool.prompt: Idea: magnets pull iron. Which example fits?
choices: An iron nail
A plastic ruler
Kitchen foil
pool.hint: Which one is made of iron? Not every metal is iron.
pool.explain: An iron nail sticks. Plastic does not, and foil is a metal that is not iron, so it does not stick either.

pool.prompt: Leo says the teacher's exact words {n} times. Has he explained it?
choices: No, a strong explanation needs the idea, his own example and why
Yes, saying it more makes it an explanation
Yes, if he says it loudly
pool.hint: Think of the three boxes about melting ice. Was any of that copied?
pool.explain: Saying it {n} times is still copying. A strong explanation has the idea, your own example and why it happens.

pool.prompt: Raj says, "My teacher told me so." Is that an explanation?
choices: No, it says who told him, not why
Yes, teachers are always right
Yes, it is the best kind
pool.hint: Does it say why the idea is true?
pool.explain: It names who told him but gives no reason. An explanation says why.

pool.prompt: You learned {n} things about the Moon. You can only teach three. What should you pick?
choices: The three ideas that matter most
The first three you heard
The funniest three
pool.hint: What did you put on Teddy's card about bees?
pool.explain: Out of {n}, pick the key ideas that help someone understand the Moon, not just any three.

pool.prompt: Why does teaching it back help you learn?
choices: Explaining shows what you know and what you do not
It is quicker than learning
It means you never forget anything
pool.hint: What did Pip find out while teaching Teddy?
pool.explain: Putting it in your own words checks your understanding and shows the gaps. It does not make you remember everything forever.

visual.caption: Is this teaching it back? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: teach Teddy in your own words, build an explanation, find the gap when Teddy asks why, test your own examples on a magnet and pick the key ideas.
